analysis.one_liner: Regulates debt settlement companies with written contracts, fee caps, and consumer refunds.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would cap debt settlement fees and force companies to earn them, died in the Senate Banking Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set national rules for companies that promise to negotiate down a person's credit card and other debts. It required a written contract, capped the fees companies could charge, barred collecting most fees until a debt was actually settled, required customer money to be held in an insured trust account, let consumers cancel at any time with refunds, and let the FTC and state attorneys general sue violators. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers in financial distress who turn to debt settlement companies. The bill would stop providers from charging large upfront and monthly fees, allow them to charge only a $50 enrollment fee and a settlement fee capped at 5% of the savings, and let them collect that fee only after a creditor actually agrees to settle. It would require honest disclosure of costs, timelines, and credit damage; require customer funds to sit in a federally insured trust account the company cannot touch; give consumers the right to cancel at any time with refunds; and give consumers, the FTC, and state attorneys general the power to sue for violations with statutory and punitive damages.

how_it_helps.text: Providers could charge only an enrollment fee (capped at $50) and a settlement fee (capped at 5% of the savings), and could not collect a settlement fee until a creditor actually agreed to settle — replacing the upfront-fee model where consumers paid thousands and often got nothing.

Consumer money had to sit in a federally insured trust account not affiliated with the provider, and consumers could cancel at any time with refunds — protecting savings from being spent by the company.

Providers had to give an individualized financial analysis and show the program offered a net tangible benefit and was suitable for the consumer, plus disclose that the consumer remains liable to creditors while in the program and that credit may be harmed.

Advertising claims about debt reduction results had to match actual average results verified by independent audit covering at least 80% of customers, and violations carried statutory damages of $1,000 to $5,000 plus punitive damages and attorneys' fees, enforceable by consumers, the FTC, and state attorneys general.

analysis.who_pays: Debt settlement providers, who would lose the ability to collect upfront and monthly fees and would face disclosure, trust-account, advertising, and civil-liability requirements. Some providers might exit the market or shrink their services rather than operate under the fee caps.

drawbacks.text: Capping the enrollment fee at $50 and the settlement fee at 5% of the savings could make it unprofitable for companies to serve consumers with small debts, shrinking access to a service some debtors use.
Requiring providers to hold funds in independent insured trust accounts and to disclose realistic timelines and credit damage raises compliance costs that smaller providers may not absorb.

Debt settlement itself — even regulated — still requires consumers to stop paying creditors, which the bill's own disclosure requirements acknowledge can hurt credit scores, invite lawsuits and garnishment, and increase what the consumer owes through interest and fees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections are real and well-targeted: pay-for-results fees, insured trust accounts, honest disclosures, and private enforcement are the fixes regulators had identified for an industry with a documented pattern of taking upfront fees and leaving consumers worse off. The strongest objections are (1) capping enrollment fees at $50 and settlement fees at 5% of savings might make it uneconomic to serve smaller debts, shrinking an option some debtors value; (2) compliance costs would push many providers out; and (3) settlement itself can damage credit and create tax liability, and the bill's disclosures flag this without preventing it. On balance the bill traded some industry convenience for substantial consumer protection, a trade most consumers in these programs would likely accept.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced by Senator Schumer on April 27, 2010, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and the Senate never voted on it before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
The bill carried only one cosponsor, so it never built the visible support that might have pushed a committee to act.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt settlement companies that profit from upfront fees kept operating under the old rules; consumers in financial distress gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt settlement companies kept their upfront-fee model

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Debt Settlement Consumer Protection Act of 2010 in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Claire McCaskill
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Debt settlement industry
against.what_they_did: The for-profit debt settlement industry opposed federal fee restrictions and regulation during this period (the FTC adopted a related advance-fee ban that year over industry objections); no industry opposition to this specific bill appears in the provided sources.

sides.party_line_note: Both named sponsors were Democrats, but the bill never reached a vote, so no record shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill banned upfront and maintenance fees, capped fees at $50 to enroll plus 5% of savings actually achieved, and imposed disclosure, trust-account, advertising, and civil-liability requirements — dismantling the business model of collecting fees before any debt is settled. Consumers using these services would keep far more of their money and get refunds on cancellation.

By barring providers from purchasing debts or collecting debts themselves, the bill kept settlement companies out of the collection business; creditors would deal with consumers directly. Consumers got little direct benefit here.

The bill required consumer funds to be held in accounts at federally insured depository institutions, routing settlement savings through bank trust accounts. Consumers gained the safety of insured, independent custody of their money.

industries.industry: Nonprofit credit counseling and bankruptcy attorneys
industries.note: The bill exempted attorneys and 501(c)(3) counseling organizations and required providers to tell consumers about nonprofit counseling and bankruptcy as alternatives, potentially steering some consumers toward these services. Consumers gained from being informed of cheaper options.
